title: Conditions for health

blocks.heading: Conditions for health
blocks.text: Clean water, hygiene, an adequate diet, prevention and treatment of disease, and social conditions can influence health and life expectancy. Life expectancy is an average under the mortality conditions used, not an individual promise. Poverty can restrict food, housing and service access; stress and illness can interact with those constraints.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Water and hygiene
blocks.text:
Safe water and appropriate hygiene reduce exposure to some contamination pathways. A supply needs reliable access and protection after collection; a new water point does not help equally if distance, breakdown or unsafe handling prevents use.

Applied example: It can reduce exposure to contaminated supplies and reduce time lost obtaining water. With fewer interruptions to health and available time, people may attend school or work more consistently.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Adequate diet
blocks.text:
A nutritionally adequate diet provides suitable energy and nutrients for health. Availability, affordability and varied intake matter. More food by weight does not necessarily establish adequate nutrition, and a household label does not diagnose nutritional status.

Applied example: People need suitable nutrients as well as enough energy. A household may obtain a large amount of one food while lacking the variety needed for an adequate diet.

blocks.heading: Disease prevention and care
blocks.text:
Prevention and effective accessible care can reduce illness and its consequences. Facilities, trained staff, supplies and timely referral must work together. A building without operating support does not establish useful health provision.

Applied example: A building provides space, but qualified workers deliver and refer care. Without operating staff, the extra physical facility need not provide usable treatment.

blocks.heading: Poverty and stress
blocks.text:
Material hardship can limit adequate food, housing and service access, while insecurity and stress can affect well-being. Illness can also reduce earnings and add care costs. Explain interacting pathways without assuming poverty establishes an individual’s health or assigning blame.

Applied example: Limited income can restrict food and access to care. Illness can then interrupt earnings and add care costs, making those material constraints harder to overcome.

blocks.heading: Follow the mechanism
blocks.text: In an invented settlement, a reliable protected water supply is paired with maintained toilets and handwashing facilities. These measures can reduce exposure to some water-borne infections through different routes. They do not prevent every disease: malaria, for example, has a mosquito transmission route. Match the prevention measure to the route and check whether the facilities remain usable.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Disease, prevention and productive participation
blocks.text: Illness can interrupt attendance at school and work, add caring time and absorb household income. Malaria is caused by a parasite transmitted through bites of infected mosquitoes; it is not caused by drinking dirty water. Safe water, sanitation and hygiene instead reduce exposure to infections associated with faecal contamination, including cholera. Mosquito control and reducing bites address a different transmission route. Match prevention to the route rather than presenting one measure as protection against all diseases. Immunisation uses vaccines to develop protection against particular infections; it is not treatment for every existing illness. Programmes need trained personnel, dependable supplies, suitable storage and reachable services. This is a development explanation, not personal diagnosis or a vaccination schedule.
context_tags: Codex repair after independent review; original teaching synthesis

blocks.heading: Worked percentage change
blocks.text: Percentage change compares a change with the starting value. Subtract the old value from the new value, divide that difference by the old value, then multiply by 100. If attendance rises from 80 to 100 users, the increase is 20 users; 20 divided by 80 is 0.25, giving 25% growth. If it falls from 100 to 80, the change is −20 users; dividing by the original 100 gives −0.2, or a 20% fall. The different denominators explain the different percentages. Percentage points instead subtract two percentages, such as coverage rising from 40% to 55%, a gain of 15 points. Starting from zero makes this percentage-change division undefined; report the absolute change.
